vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 39-year-old Tongan-New Zealand man, now living alone in a studio apartment outside Seattle following a divorce that finalised eight months ago. He has flown commercial aircraft for fourteen years, accumulating the kind of quiet authority that comes with long experience - a man accustomed to reading environments for risk and keeping others calm under pressure. That professional identity has become one of the central ironies of his current suffering, because since an encounter with police fourteen months ago, he has found himself unable to trust his own threat assessments, unable to feel safe in proximity to other people, and barely able to hold the memory of what happened without it flooding back as though it were still occurring.

The incident took place on a late evening in a supermarket parking lot. Rangi had been returning to his car when two officers approached him without warning, weapons drawn, shouting commands he struggled at first to parse. He was forced to the ground, handcuffed, and held there for nearly twenty minutes while a case of mistaken identity was slowly unravelled. No one apologised. What stayed with him was not only the terror of the guns but the specific texture of that moment - the hard asphalt against his cheek, the sound of footsteps behind him before he understood what was happening, the nauseating surge of adrenaline that did not subside even after the officers walked away. He drove home shaking, pulled over twice to be sick, and told no one.

The memories that formed from that night carry a quality Rangi finds deeply disorienting. They do not feel like recollections - they feel more real and vivid than anything else in his life, more present than his daughter's last birthday or his first solo flight, as though that parking lot exists in higher resolution than the rest of his history. And yet the event itself feels simultaneously impossible to believe - so extreme, so out of proportion with a Tuesday evening, that he sometimes catches himself thinking it could not really have happened to him. When he does remember it, the terror returns wholesale, not as an echo but as the thing itself, and it is this quality of the memory - its aliveness, its refusal to recede - that keeps pulling him back into a state of vigilance he cannot switch off. The memory does not stay in the past; it bleeds forward, making ordinary moments feel like precursors to something catastrophic, and it is in this way that the recollections themselves have become a source of ongoing threat rather than a closed chapter.

In the months that followed, Rangi's body began registering danger in patterns that bore the shape of that night. Physical proximity to strangers - anyone moving into his personal space without announcement - triggers an immediate spike of alarm, the same alarm the footsteps produced before the officers appeared. Nausea, which had accompanied his body's response that evening, now returns in those same moments of proximity, a somatic echo he cannot reason away. Driving with passengers in the vehicle has become nearly intolerable; the presence of another person beside him reactivates something he cannot name but cannot ignore. These triggers do not merely cause discomfort - they restore the full architecture of threat he experienced that night, convincing him that danger is present and imminent. Strangers approaching him in ordinary situations, a colleague walking toward him in a corridor, a gate agent crossing the jetway - each one reads to him as a potential threat, and he is certain this is not paranoia but accurate perception. When something takes longer than expected - a delayed clearance, a passenger who hasn't boarded - he assumes something bad is unfolding. Ordinary sounds make him flinch in ways his crew have begun to notice.

The threat he feels in these moments does not stay contained. It circles back, pulling up the memory again with renewed force, and the memory in turn makes the next encounter with a stranger or a sound feel more dangerous than the last. His ex-wife had grown exhausted by what she called his inability to be present; the divorce, while not caused solely by this, accelerated after the incident. He now avoids ride-shares, has declined several long-haul pairings to avoid confined cockpits with unfamiliar co-pilots, and has not told his employer why.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a near-incident during descent into Portland - a moment where a sudden radio burst made him freeze for two seconds longer than he should have. He is most afraid that he is no longer safe to fly. What he hopes, quietly, is that someone can explain why his own mind has become the thing he cannot trust.
